question: A new oral antibiotic has excellent in-vitro activity against drug-resistant organisms and is available at very low cost. However, clinical trial data come only from small Phase II studies in high-income settings. Which WHO/NLEM criterion does this drug FAIL to meet for essential medicine status?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cost data may actually support listing, but affordability alone is not the criterion at issue here. The problem is with the evidence base, not the price.

answers.text: Evidence of efficacy and safety from adequate clinical trials in the relevant population

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. WHO essential medicine selection requires clinical evidence from well-conducted trials in populations relevant to the intended use setting. Small Phase II trials in dissimilar populations do not satisfy this criterion.

answers.text: Availability as a single active ingredient formulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Single-ingredient preference is a secondary consideration for fixed-dose combinations, not the primary criterion relevant here.

answers.text: Public health relevance and burden of disease in the country

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Activity against resistant organisms suggests public health relevance exists. The criterion actually failing is evidence quality, not disease relevance.

overallFeedback.feedback: Re-read the WHO/NLEM selection framework. The question highlights a gap in clinical evidence quality — the key criterion being tested is proven efficacy and safety from adequate trials in the relevant population.

Well done. The three core criteria for essential medicine selection are: (1) public health relevance, (2) proven efficacy and safety from adequate trials in the target population, and (3) cost-effectiveness. This drug fails on criterion 2.
